title: Reforming the Judiciary -- Ch. 17: Republic v. Cocofed: Coco Levies Are Prima Facie Public Funds
primary_topics: Chapter 17 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' -- CJP's presentation of Republic v. Cocofed, the December 14, 2001 Decision he wrote for the Court holding that the sequestered controlling shares in the United Coconut Planters Bank should be voted by the government because they were purchased with coconut levy funds that are prima facie public in character.

The chapter's reprinting, with permission, of former Senate President Jovito R. Salonga's Kilosbayan summation of the case, written by the man who as first PCGG chair had sequestered the shares in the first place.

The doctrinal core of the ruling: the general rule that registered owners vote their shares, the two-tiered test for sequestered shares alleged to be ill-gotten, and the 'public character' exceptions from BASECO and Cojuangco, Jr. v. Roxas under which the government votes shares that were originally government-owned or bought with public funds.

The six itemized reasons the Court gave for holding coco levies public -- their exaction under the police and taxing powers, the judicial admission that the shares were bought with them, COA review, BIR treatment, and the decrees themselves -- together with the caveat limiting the ruling to the voting question and the order that the Sandiganbayan decide the main cases within six months.
sub_topics: CJP introduces the case as one of the most important decisions of his seventh year in office, notes that he 'had the honor of writing' it for the Court, and explains that control of UCPB would pass to the government as trustee for more than one million coconut farmers from whom the levies had been exacted under Marcos.
He states that Salonga, the first chair of the PCGG that sequestered the shares, wrote an extensive summation which he is reprinting from the January 2002 issue of Kilosbayan magazine.

Salonga opens with the December 14, 2001 divided vote, the government's continued voting of the shares pending reversion, the main case pending in the Sandiganbayan since July 31, 1987, and the Court's order that the Sandiganbayan decide with finality within six months and report every three months on pain of contempt.
He defines prima facie -- 'at first sight' or 'on the face of it' -- as evidence good and sufficient on its face that prevails until contradicted and overcome by better evidence.

He recounts the PCGG's first post-EDSA trip to the United States: the State Department's delivery of 2,300 Malacanang documents impounded in Honolulu, his testimony before the Solarz Committee and by deposition in New York, and his Los Angeles meeting on March 28, 1986 with Eduardo 'Danding' Cojuangco, who promised a full written disclosure through his lawyer that was never submitted.

He traces the sequestration under Executive Orders 1, 2 and 14 of the Cojuangco firms and the UCPB shares registered to the alleged one million coconut farmers, the CIIF companies and Cojuangco, and lists the Marcos decrees that imposed the levy and the coconut monopolies.

He follows the procedural history: the Sandiganbayan's November 15, 1990 lifting of sequestration for failure to implead the private respondents, the PCGG's certiorari petition in GR No. 96073, the TRO over the UCPB board election, and the February 16, 1993 resolution that the respondents' right to vote 'still has to be established by them before the Sandiganbayan.'

He records the January 23, 1995 Narvasa Decision nullifying the lifting of sequestration and holding that the companies are 'simply the res' in actions to recover illegally acquired wealth, so impleading them was unnecessary.

He describes the 2001 flashpoint: the ACCRA Law Office's February 13, 2001 demand for a stockholders' meeting on behalf of COCOFED and the nameless one million farmers, the Class Action Omnibus Motion to enjoin the PCGG from voting, the Sandiganbayan's February 28, 2001 Order, and the PCGG's petition for certiorari.

He notes the referral from the 3rd Division, which had split 3-2, to the Court en banc, and the oral argument in Baguio City on April 17, 2001 where the issue was framed as whether the Sandiganbayan gravely abused its discretion.

He quotes the holding that the government should continue voting the shares because they were bought with funds 'prima facie public in character or, at the very least, affected with public interest,' and the Court's resolve to be 'more categorical and positive than its earlier pronouncements.'

He sets out the reasoning in numbered steps: the general rule that the registered owner votes; the PCGG as mere conservator; the two-tiered test of prima facie ill-gotten character plus imminent danger of dissipation; and the two public-character exceptions carved out in BASECO and Cojuangco-Roxas.

He supplies the documented BASECO facts -- the 1972 incorporation, the acquisitions from NASSCO and the Export Processing Authority, the NDC and GSIS loans, Captain A.T. Romualdez's reports -- and the 1986 finding that Marcos 'actually owns well nigh one hundred percent of its outstanding capital stock.'

He quotes Justice Ameurfina Melencio Herrera's concurrence, joined by Justice Feliciano, allowing the vote of sequestered stock where a business actually belonging to the government or capitalized from public funds 'somehow landed in private hands.'

He summarizes the resulting rule: the two-tiered test applies to shares merely alleged to be ill-gotten, but not where the shares are shown prima facie to have been originally government shares or purchased with public funds, in which case the public character exceptions prevail and the government votes.

He records the undisputed fact, admitted by respondents' counsel at the April 17, 2001 oral argument, that the money used to buy the UCPB shares came from the Coconut Consumers Stabilization Fund, and the 1989 Cocofed v. PCGG declaration to the same effect under PD 755.

He answers the argument that the 1993 resolution became functus officio after the 1995 decision, and asks why the respondents waited six years to assert a right they claimed the 1995 decision had granted them.

He lists the Court's six reasons why coco levies are public funds: they were raised through the police and taxing powers under PD 276, PD 961 and PD 1468; they were levies imposed for the benefit of the coconut industry; the respondents judicially admitted the shares were bought with public funds; COA reviews their use; the BIR has treated them as public; and the decrees themselves -- including PD 771 and PD 1234 -- treat them as special funds in the National Treasury.

He adds the detail that Marcos himself crossed out and initialed the deletion of the phrase 'which is a private fund of the coconut farmers,' manifesting the legislative intent to regard the fund as public.

He notes the procedural holding of grave abuse of discretion for departing from BASECO and Cojuangco-Roxas, and the Court's authority to pass on an unassigned error on which the assigned questions depend.

He sets out the caveat: the determination is merely prima facie, it does not classify the funds as general, trust or special, and it does not settle whether Cojuangco's shares came from private enterprise -- the only issue settled being the PCGG's right to vote pending the main cases.

He closes the majority discussion with the fifteen-year delay since 1986-87, the order that the Sandiganbayan decide within six months and report every three months on pain of contempt, and the roll of concurring justices.

He reprints the Melo dissent, joined in result by Kapunan, Pardo, Ynares-Santiago and Sandoval-Gutierrez, arguing that BASECO is distinguishable because Marcos's near-total ownership there was proven, that respondents here are registered stockholders whose acquisitions are precisely what the main case will test, that ruling now preempts the Sandiganbayan on the lis mota, and that no grave abuse can lie on an issue never raised below.

He reprints Justice Vitug's separate opinion, joined by Justice Puno, on tax proceeds being usable only for a public purpose and payable only by appropriation, and on Cojuangco's two 1975 agreements, concluding that pending a conclusive determination it would be neither right nor just to deprive him of voting roughly ten percent of the equity.

stances.claim: The controlling UCPB shares should be voted by the government, because they were purchased with coconut levy funds that are prima facie public in character or at the very least affected with public interest.
stances.rhetorical_move: ponente's holding stated categorically -- the Court declaring itself 'more categorical and positive than its earlier pronouncements'

stances.claim: Coconut levy funds are public funds, being raised through the police and taxing powers, admitted by respondents to have bought the shares, audited by COA, treated as public by the BIR, and declared special funds of the National Treasury by the decrees themselves.
stances.rhetorical_move: six-point itemization of independent grounds, capped by Marcos's own deletion of the phrase calling the fund private

stances.claim: The two-tiered test governs only shares merely alleged to be ill-gotten; where shares are shown prima facie to be originally government shares or bought with public funds, the public character exceptions of BASECO and Cojuangco-Roxas control and the government votes them.
stances.rhetorical_move: doctrinal sorting -- separating two lines of precedent and assigning each its domain, so the Sandiganbayan's contrary application becomes grave abuse

stances.claim: Public property registered in the names of non-owners is affected with trust relations, because legal fiction must yield to truth and the prima facie beneficial owner should enjoy the rights of ownership.
stances.rhetorical_move: appeal to a 'common-sense principle' underlying the precedents rather than to text alone

stances.claim: The ruling is expressly limited: it is merely prima facie, does not classify the funds, does not resolve Cojuangco's claim of private enterprise, and settles only who may vote pending the main cases.
stances.rhetorical_move: self-limiting caveat appended to the holding, paired with a deadline and reporting duty imposed on the Sandiganbayan

stances.claim: BASECO is distinguishable and the majority preempts the Sandiganbayan, since the validity of the respondents' acquisitions is the very lis mota of the pending reconveyance case and the public-funds argument was never raised below.
stances.rhetorical_move: reported from Justice Melo's dissent, joined in result by four other justices

stances.claim: Cojuangco should meanwhile be allowed to vote the roughly ten percent equity he claims to have retained, pending a conclusive determination of the legality of that retention.

notable_anecdotes: The Honolulu documents: Salonga recounts the State Department delivering 2,300 documents the Marcoses had carried from Malacanang, impounded by Customs in Honolulu, to the PCGG on March 18, 1986.

The meeting in Los Angeles: on March 28, 1986 a friend arranged for Danding Cojuangco to see Salonga, who listened with the least interruption and asked for a full written disclosure through Cojuangco's lawyer -- a disclosure never submitted before Salonga left the PCGG.

Marcos's pen stroke: the Court noted that Marcos himself crossed out the phrase 'which is a private fund of the coconut farmers' and initialed the deletion, shown as an attachment to the petitioner's memorandum.
The six-year silence: Salonga asks why, if the respondents believed the 1995 decision gave them the right to vote, they waited six years before demanding a stockholders' meeting in 2001.

Fifteen years and a deadline: with the cases pending since the Aquino administration, the Court ordered the Sandiganbayan to decide within six months and report every three months on pain of contempt.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 17 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' presented Republic v. Cocofed, which CJP identified as one of the most important decisions of his seventh year on the Court and which he 'had the honor of writing.' The ruling held that the controlling sequestered shares in the United Coconut Planters Bank should be voted by the government, because they had been bought with coconut levy funds exacted from more than a million farmers during the Marcos regime -- funds the Court declared 'not only affected with public interest' but 'in fact, prima facie public funds.' Rather than restate the case himself, CJP reprinted with permission the Kilosbayan summation written by former Senate President Jovito R. Salonga, the first PCGG chair, who had sequestered the shares. Salonga defined prima facie for lay readers, recounted the PCGG's 1986 recovery mission and his own Los Angeles meeting with Eduardo Cojuangco, and traced fifteen years of litigation from the 1987 reconveyance suit through the 1990 lifting of sequestration, the 1993 resolution, the 1995 Narvasa decision, and the 2001 demand for a stockholders' meeting that produced the assailed Sandiganbayan order. He then laid out the reasoning step by step: registered owners normally vote, the PCGG is a mere conservator, sequestered shares alleged to be ill-gotten are tested by the two-tiered test of prima facie ill-gotten character and imminent dissipation, but shares shown to be originally governmental or bought with public funds fall instead under the public character exceptions of BASECO and Cojuangco-Roxas, on the principle that 'legal fiction must yield to truth.' Since respondents' counsel had judicially admitted the shares came from the Coconut Consumers Stabilization Fund, the Court itemized six reasons the levies were public -- the police and taxing powers, the purpose of the levy, the admission, COA review, BIR treatment and the decrees themselves, with Marcos's own deletion of the words calling the fund private. The Court added a caveat limiting the ruling to the voting question and ordered the Sandiganbayan to decide the main cases within six months. Salonga then reprinted Justice Melo's dissent and Justice Vitug's partial dissent.
